transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-01
Start: 15:30 PST
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Liu (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Sofia Moreno (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Orbit CTO), Luca Romano (Infra), Priya Singh (ML)

[00:00] Jamie Liu: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, appreciate you taking the time. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Maya Chen: Maya here.
[00:08] Luca Romano: Luca on call.
[00:09] Priya Singh: Priya here.
[00:11] Jamie Liu: Great. I'll kick off with the objective — scope a short POC to validate capacity and autoscale behavior for your realtime inference path. Specifically reserved GPUs plus burst pool and fallback policies.
[00:24] Ravi Patel: Hi team, I'm Ravi, I'll be the SE on the trial. We'll walk through success criteria and a benchmark plan.
[00:30] Maya Chen: Quick context from us — we're building biometric transcription + response flow, typical request size ~400-600 tokens, sometimes up to 1k. Peak TPS is spiky: 120 rps for 2-3 minutes, otherwise 8-12 rps. Critical is p95 latency under 200ms for the 512 token path. Cost also matters, we have strict budget for pilot.
[00:52] Jamie Liu: Got it. That p95 <200ms target is reasonable to aim for with reserved GPUs and KV cache, we'll need to size the reserved pool accordingly. A couple clarifying questions: do you need private deployment in a V P C for this POC or is hosted ok for the initial runs?
[01:10] Maya Chen: We prefer private VPC for the benchmark so network egress and residency mimic prod. We'll provide a test subnet.
[01:16] Jamie Liu: Perfect — we'll need a service account and limited IP whitelisting.
[01:20] Luca Romano: We'll provision that. Also, what about keys and K M S integration? We need to validate CMK wrapping later but for pilot, simple customer-managed KMS token is fine.
[01:32] Sofia Moreno: Noted. For the POC we can accept a temp key but will document how CMK works for Private.
[01:38] Priya Singh: From modeling side, we plan to run the 7B open model and a quantized 4-bit variant for fallbacks. Can Redwood run both and route automatically?
[01:48] Ravi Patel: Yes — Redwood can host model variants and route per policy. Typical fallback order we propose: 1) try reserved full-precision model on pool; 2) if capacity blocked, spill to quantized variant on the same pool; 3) if still constrained, burst to hosted GPUs (if allowed); 4) last resort: degrade features — reduce max tokens or offload heavy functions. We can tune priority and max burst concurrency.
[02:12] Maya Chen: That ordering makes sense. Two related asks: can we enforce a hard budget cap on burst? And can we set a warm pre-warmed queue so the first request doesn't see cold-starts?
[02:24] Ravi Patel: Yes to both. You can set burst caps (concurrency tokens or $ caps) and pre-warm small pool. For the POC we'd recommend a reserved baseline sized to handle median load with a burst pool for 30-60 spare concurrent slots.
[02:40] Jamie Liu: For sizing, we used your traffic numbers — median 10 rps, peaks 120 rps. If we assume a 7B model serving ~12 rps per GPU at your 512-token average (rough estimate), to handle 120 rps consistently without burst you'd need 10 GPUs. For a cost-conscious POC we recommend 3-4 reserved GPUs + burst pool of 6 GPUs and explicit fallback thresholds. That lets us validate both normal and degraded behavior.
[03:10] Luca Romano: Can you show the math again? The 12 rps per GPU is optimistic. Our payloads sometimes have long context.
[03:18] Ravi Patel: Sure — it's a starting point; we will run a quick micro-benchmark with your sample traces to get empirical rps/GPU. The plan: we run an initial baseline benchmark (synthetic) to measure tokens/sec and latency per GPU for both 7B and quantized 4-bit. Then we run replay traces to see how burst behaves.
[03:36] Maya Chen: Timeline for the POC? We're hoping to complete in two weeks.
[03:40] Jamie Liu: Two-week pilot is typical. Week 1: set up VPC + model onboarding + run baseline micro-benchmarks (1-2 days) and a stress window (2-3 hours) with the burst pool enabled. Week 2: soak run with failure injection (evict some reserved nodes) and run replay tests, then a 1-hour review with results and recommendations.
[03:58] Priya Singh: Failure injection — like killing GPUs to see fallback?
[04:01] Ravi Patel: Exactly. We'll simulate node failures and capacity exhaustion to ensure fallback ordering and degraded modes behave predictably. We'll also verify KV cache sharing and prefix caching benefits for repeated requests.
[04:12] Luca Romano: About KV cache — does Redwood share KV across nodes or is it local?
[04:17] Sofia Moreno: Currently cache is local to the serving instance but we have a prefix cache layer that can persist between warm instances for common prefixes. There are tradeoffs for consistency; we'll document the exact behavior in the runbook (and sorry if earlier docs called it K V cache, transcription flag).
[04:32] Maya Chen: Security checklist: SOC2, SAML SSO, audit logs for token-level tracing, and encryption at rest with customer KMS. Can you commit to those for Private deployment?
[04:44] Jamie Liu: Yes, Private includes SOC2 controls, SAML SSO support, audit logs — we'll share the SOC2 report and integration guide. For CMK we'll outline how HSM-backed keys are used.
[04:56] Priya Singh: For benchmarks, we want p95 and p99 latencies, cost per 1k tokens, and model quality delta when falling back to quantized variant. How do you suggest measuring quality?
[05:08] Ravi Patel: Two approaches: 1) automated evals on a held-out prompt set (we'll compute similarity metrics and hallucination rate), 2) manual spot-checks for critical flows. We'll provide scripts to run both. Expect some quality delta with 4-bit quantization — we'll quantify that and identify prompts sensitive to degradation.
[05:28] Jamie Liu: Also we'll instrument token-level breakdowns in the console so you can see where time is spent (decode vs kernel). That helps root-cause for slow tails.
[05:36] Maya Chen: Good. One more question — how deterministic is the burst latency when bursting to hosted GPUs in another region? We worry about network variability.
[05:45] Ravi Patel: There is extra network hop cost. For private VPC bursts we'll prefer same-region hosts, and we can limit burst to the same AZ when possible. We'll measure network P95 during the benchmark and factor that into recommendations.
[06:00] Luca Romano: Pricing — can you provide an example cost for this 2-week pilot including reserved commit?
[06:05] Jamie Liu: We'll send a tailored reserved quote. For the pilot we can do a short-term reserved pool with a trial discount and an explicit cap on burst spend. We'll include cost-per-1k tokens and estimated monthly if you extrapolate to production.
[06:17] Maya Chen: Ok. On observability, need per-route dashboards and tracing hooks so our engineers can tie requests back to logs.
[06:25] Sofia Moreno: That's included in Redwood Console for Private. We'll add the tracing hook snippet to the runbook.
[06:30] Jamie Liu: Let's quickly outline the benchmark plan and success criteria — call back to screen share? we won't screen-share now but I'll read it out.
[06:38] Ravi Patel: (reads) Baseline micro-benchmarks: 3 token profiles — 256, 512, 1024; measure p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec per GPU. Replay test: run 2-hour trace replay with spikes up to 120 rps, observe fallback counts and burst duration. Soak test: 24-hour lower-intensity run to observe memory leak / queueing. Success criteria: p95 <= 200ms for 512 tokens on reserved+cache for at least 95% of the time during normal load; fallback rate under 5% for median traffic; quantized fallback quality drop within acceptable threshold (TBD by Priya).
[07:12] Priya Singh: For quality threshold, we'll set an automated n-gram overlap and a manual check that critical intents remain intact. I'll send a 200-prompt sample.
[07:21] Jamie Liu: Perfect. Next, fallback policy specifics — we'll propose default settings and you can tweak. Also we'll set a hard budget cap to stop burst when cost hits cap and send alerts.
[07:33] Luca Romano: What about queueing? If burst is capped and reserved saturated, do you queue or reject?
[07:39] Ravi Patel: You can choose: 1) queue with backpressure and an SLA on max queueing latency, 2) reject with a 429 so client can retry, or 3) fallback to a cheaper predict mode. For low-latency use cases we'd recommend rejecting quickly so the client UX can show a graceful degraded response.
[07:56] Maya Chen: We'll want a short queue window (200-300ms) then reject.
[08:00] Jamie Liu: Noted. We'll include config snippets in the runbook.
[08:04] Maya Chen: Any gotchas we should prepare for?
[08:07] Ravi Patel: Cold-starts on large models can be painful if you don't have pre-warmed instances; also KV cache miss rates can spike token compute. We suggest priming common prefixes and enabling continuous batching for small requests. Also watch for long context windows that change GPU throughput.
[08:26] Priya Singh: For our replay we have a lot of context hops with user history; caching might help a lot.
[08:31] Sofia Moreno: We'll instrument how prefix hit-rate impacts latency in the console.
[08:35] Jamie Liu: OK let's summarize next steps: we'll send the POC runbook with exact benchmark commands, a reserved capacity quote with burst caps, and security docs. You (Orbit) will provide test VPC credentials and the replay trace (Priya to send). We'll schedule the benchmark window next Wednesday 11/4 10am-12pm PT.
[08:56] Maya Chen: That works for us.
[09:00] Luca Romano: I'll get the VPC role and whitelist ready.
[09:03] Jamie Liu: Great. Any final questions?
[09:05] Priya Singh: One last smaller ask — can Redwood produce an initial rough estimate of rps/GPU using our 512 token avg prior to the benchmark? Even a conservative number helps plan.
[09:15] Ravi Patel: We'll run a quick internal micro test today using representative samples and send an initial rps/GPU estimate; mark it conservative.
[09:22] Jamie Liu: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the runbook, quote, and benchmark invite.
[09:27] Meeting end.

Notes about transcript: occasional mis-heard acronyms (K V cache, V P C) and minor stutters — cleaned lightly but left in filler words to preserve authenticity.
